cards.title: Source winning ad concepts from competitors' longest-running ads
cards.summary: Find proven creative concepts by scanning the Facebook Ad Library or a tool like Magic Brief for competitors' longest-running, highest-spend ads.
cards.use_when: You need new ad concepts to test for your store and are deciding where to source creative inspiration.
steps: Open Facebook Ad Library, click 'All Ads,' and search each of your most relevant competitors by page name. Set active status to 'All' so paused ads also appear, since some competitors run ads across multiple pages.

Identify ads that have been live the longest or spent the most. Source advice: avoid anything marked 'low impression count' since that signals it is not performing, and scroll to ads that have run for the longest time period.

Optionally use a paid tool like Magic Brief (verify current name/interface) to view an aggregate of a competitor's active ads across pages and to filter more easily. The free Ad Library route requires searching each page separately.
Treat each long-running ad as a distinct concept, not a template to copy identically. Note it and plan to extrapolate dozens of variations for your own products.
Build a collection spanning formats — videos, statics, GIFs, carousels — and look for common threads that repeat across multiple competitors in your category.
Pick comparison brands one or two steps above your own size (e.g., if you do $1M, study a $10M brand), not category giants, so their concepts are achievable for your budget and catalog.
caveats: The source says not to compare a small brand to Lululemon or Nike; oversized benchmarks distort what is realistic.
Ad Library may split a competitor's activity across several pages, so results can be incomplete.
Longevity and spend are proxies for performance, not proof of profitability.

cards.title: Recreate competitor concepts as your own catalog variations
cards.summary: Turn a competitor's winning concept into a large batch of on-brand iterations across your own products rather than a single copy.
cards.use_when: You have identified a competitor ad that has run a long time and want to convert it into testable creative for your store's catalog.
steps: Take the winning competitor concept and re-shoot or re-design it with your product and brand assets — do not reuse their files.

If it is a proven concept, rebuild it for every applicable product in your catalog, not just one SKU. The source example: recreate a Lululemon carousel for a competing athleisure brand for each product.

Produce dozens of distinct variations per concept rather than copying your own best-performing ad. The source stresses new concepts, iterations, and variations as three different things, matching current Meta/Andromeda algorithmic behavior.
Spread the variations across formats the competitor used (video, static, GIF, carousel) to test concept and format simultaneously.
Keep a running concept library so each new ad maps to a known concept rather than being ad-hoc.
caveats: The source frames this as increasing win rate versus mass-producing low-quality UGC; volume alone is not the goal.
Copying creative too literally risks brand and legal issues — treat competitor ads as inspiration for the concept, not assets to clone.
Source advice is presenter opinion on how current Meta delivery works and may change with platform updates.

cards.title: Launch new ads as isolated 'packs' inside a prospecting CBO campaign
cards.summary: Group each batch of new creatives into its own ad set in a CBO prospecting campaign so new concepts compete with each other on the same budget.
cards.use_when: You are setting up campaign structure to test a new batch of creative concepts and deciding how to organize ad sets.
steps: Run all new creative inside one prospecting CBO (campaign budget optimization) campaign so the algorithm allocates across ad sets.
Every time you have a batch of new creatives, put them into a brand-new ad set — a 'pack' — rather than adding them to an existing ad set.
Batch 4 to 8 creatives per pack as the source's stated sweet spot, though anywhere from 1 to 15 is workable. Keep it simple rather than over-engineering.
Expect many ad sets over time — the source example shows a brand running past 'Broadpack 76' after continuous testing.
Do not treat the pack structure as fixed forever; the source notes nuances exist depending on product, category, and business setup.
caveats: The source is describing Meta's CBO prospecting setup as of this recording; verify current campaign options in Ads Manager.
Grouping by product or category instead of all-at-once is presented as a legitimate alternative, not an error.

cards.title: Force early spend on new ads with a 1x-CPA ad set minimum
cards.summary: Set an ad set minimum daily spend equal to 1x your target CPA for 7 days to prevent new creatives from starving behind older winning ads.
cards.use_when: New ad sets are getting almost no delivery because older ads hog the budget, and you need to test them quickly.
steps: In Ads Manager, go to the ad set's Budget & Schedule section and click 'Ad set spending limits.'
Choose 'Set a minimum or maximum,' switch the percent value to a dollar value, and enter an average daily minimum equal to 1x your target cost per acquisition (e.g., target CPA of $50 → $50 minimum).
Keep the minimum on for a maximum of 7 days at a time. Set a calendar reminder or alarm so you actually return to review it — the source says these never stay on longer than 7 days.

After 7 days, decide per ad set: if the creative is spending above the minimum, leave it running (a winner will keep spending above the floor even if you remove it); if it is only spending at the floor, remove the minimum so it drops spend, or kill it.
Reassess and reapply for the next pack of new creatives.
caveats: The 1x-CPA and 7-day limits are the source's specific heuristics, not platform-enforced rules or universal benchmarks.
If you keep the minimum on a losing ad set it will continue spending at that level — most cases the source advises against keeping it.
This forces spend; it does not guarantee the correct audience or creative quality.

cards.title: Analyze winners with incremental attribution and a spend/ROAS threshold
cards.summary: Review ad performance using incremental attribution, sort by spend, and flag high-spend ads that beat your brand's ROAS threshold as iteration candidates.
cards.use_when: You are running the analysis step of a creative testing cycle and deciding which ads to iterate or scale.
steps: In the prospecting campaign, open the column set, go to Compare Attribution Settings, and select incremental attribution.
Sort the account by highest spend to lowest spend. The source notes you may instead break the view into groups by product or category depending on your business.

Identify ads that are simultaneously high-spend, above your brand's incremental ROAS threshold, and showing outsized results on that spend. The example brand required an incremental ROAS above ~1.1 for new customers; a standout ad spent $26k (over 25% of campaign spend) at 1.46.
Do not touch ads sitting right at the threshold (e.g., 1.13–1.16 in the example) — leave them for now.
Take the true standouts and feed them back into the flywheel as concepts to duplicate, vary, and iterate.
Set your threshold from your own economics — the source explicitly notes low threshold figures sound crazy but reflect what that brand can function at.
caveats: The 1.1 threshold, $26k spend, and 1.46 ROAS are one brand's example, not a benchmark to copy.
Incremental attribution differs from standard reported ROAS; compare like-for-like before judging.
Source is presenter opinion on how analysis should work under current Meta reporting.

cards.title: Iterate off your own winners to complete the creative flywheel
cards.summary: Duplicate, vary, and merge your best-performing ads the same way you do competitors, feeding results back into continuous testing.
cards.use_when: You have identified high-spend, above-threshold winning ads and want to extend their life and solidify core concepts.
steps: Take each winning ad and create duplicates, variants, and new iterations, exactly as you would when mining competitor concepts.
Create merged concepts by combining two proven concepts (the source example: concept A + concept B → concept C).
Build variant families: reuse one winning concept across collections, swapping products, model shots, or the in-between repeated shots while keeping the simple headline structure.
Run the loop continuously: source concepts → launch packs → wait → analyze incremental performance → iterate winners → source again.
As the account grows, do not fear increasing spend or re-entering the learning phase — the source frames this system as a growth engine, not a maintenance system.
caveats: Iterating indefinitely on one concept can saturate over time; the flywheel is meant to keep new concepts entering alongside iterations.
The source's examples (brand 'Talentless' running a concept for a year) are illustrations, not guaranteed outcomes.

cards.title: Judge ads by total profit across concepts, not a single top ROAS
cards.summary: Run a portfolio of concepts where profitable high-spend and lower-spend winners coexist, rather than chasing only the highest ROAS ad.
cards.use_when: You are deciding which ad concepts to keep, scale, or cut based on ROAS versus spend capacity.
steps: Map each concept's return rate against how much it can actually spend — a target 2x ROAS concept might spend $10k, a 3x concept $3k, a 10x concept only $500, and a 2.2x concept $50k.

Instead of running only the highest-ROAS ad (the source calls this 'old school' thinking versus current Meta behavior), keep every concept that is profitable at its spend level, because each adds profit.
Prioritize total contribution to your bank account over the headline ROAS number — the source argues you should care less about a 5x versus a 2x as long as the 2x is profitable.
Match each concept to the audiences it performs with best; concepts perform at different rates per audience.
Use this view when allocating budget across packs and deciding which concepts to iterate further.
caveats: Profitability depends on your true margins and costs, not on the ROAS the ad platform reports.
The specific 2x/3x/10x/$500/$50k figures are illustrative examples from the source, not benchmarks.
Presenter opinion: the 'focus on all profitable concepts' stance is current as of this recording and may shift with Meta delivery changes.

cards.title: Build a predictable creative machine instead of duplicating old ads
cards.summary: Replace ad-hoc creative production (duplicate winners or mass-produce UGC) with a repeatable system that raises the win rate of new concepts.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to keep pumping out volume-based creative or invest in a structured creative production and testing workflow.
steps: Move away from the legacy workflow of thinking of an idea, making ads similar to past ones, uploading as single image or video, and manually writing primary text, headlines, and descriptions each time.
Define the flywheel as four linked stages: source new concepts (mostly from competitors), launch new ads in isolated packs, wait through the forced-spend window, analyze incremental performance.
Feed winning ads back as new concepts to iterate, keeping concepts, iterations, and variations as distinct outputs.

Accept that you can churn out hundreds of ads cheaply (fake UGC, creator hires, self-made videos) but the source says win rate will be low; the flywheel targets a higher win rate, not just higher volume.
Treat creative iteration and testing as a standing capability the account runs continuously, similar to how the source says its team runs it across 100+ brands.
caveats: The source's results across its brand roster are its own, not a promised outcome.
System requires sustained iteration and monitoring; it is not a one-time launch.
Promotional content about the source's paid community is excluded from this card.

input.text:
10-MCR / paid social creative and content

Goes here. Paid social creative production, hook writing, direct response video frameworks, creator/UGC scripting, static ad design, messaging strategies, evaluating stages of awareness, identifying new ad formats/angles, advertorials, unique mechanisms, and creative strategist workflows.

Not here.

Paid advertising performance metrics, ROAS, scaling rules, bidding, or ad-platform specific attribution -> 11-ADC

Conversion rate optimization (CRO) on core website pages or general analytics -> 06-MEA

Header. url: rights: public_reference why: Details a systematic "creative flywheel" framework for Meta ads that combines competitor ad analysis, modular "pack-based" testing, 7-day minimum budget constraints to force algorithmic delivery, and iterative scaling of proven concepts. modules: [MCR] topics: [creative strategy, messaging and positioning, campaign setup and tracking] tier: 2 scope_hint: core

Topics. creative strategy / Building a systematic "creative flywheel" to continuously produce winning ad concepts. Sourcing high-performing creative inspiration from competitors (via Facebook Ad Library or tools like Magic Brief) by identifying ads that have been active and spending for the longest periods. Extrapolating those winning competitor concepts into dozens of distinct in-house variations and iterations tailored to your own brand and product catalog. campaign setup and tracking / Implementing a structured testing framework within a prospecting CBO campaign. Grouping new creative concepts into isolated ad sets ("packs") containing 4 to 8 ads. Applying a 7-day minimum budget constraint at the ad set level equal to 1x the target CPA to force delivery on new assets and bypass the slow-spending waiting phase. Analyzing performance using "incremental attribution" windows to isolate top-spending, profitable ads and feed them back into the creative flywheel for rapid iteration.

Look for. The primary method for finding winning creative inspiration from competitors: scanning the Ad Library or Magic Brief for ads that have been active and spending money for the longest periods. The definition of the "creative flywheel" framework: a continuous system of sourcing new concepts from competitors, launching them in modular ad sets, analyzing incremental performance, and iterating off winning ads. The recommended setup for forcing spend on new ads: setting a 7-day minimum budget equal to 1x the target CPA at the ad set level.

Skip. Promotional pitches to join the speaker's "School" community.

Scope mix. Almost all core.

Volume. 10 to 15.

In this video, I'll be breaking down the single best creative ad strategy for 2026 [music] so that you can make killer high-erforming ad creatives in Facebook ads. This is the exact creative strategy that we're deploying over our 100 plus brands at the Moonlighters and the same exact creative strategy that I've shared within my school community [music] to nearly 300 brands right now. And this will 100% work no matter what category in. Whether you're in fashion, beauty, wellness, you name it. The old school way of creating ads would be a very simple workflow. You would think of an ad idea or your media buyer would say, "Hey, we need new ads. Maybe here's what's working." Then you would go and create new ads that look similar to the ones you've created before. Or if you had a new concept, something you thought might work well, you would go ahead and create it. Then you'd come into the Facebook ads manager. You'd upload it all as a single image or video. and you'd sit here writing painfully your primary text, your headlines, your descriptions. So, what we want to do instead is creating a system that increases the likelihood of finding winning ads. You can go ahead and pump out a,000 ads in an hour. You can go ahead and make a bunch of fake UGC or hire a bunch of creators or make a bunch of videos for yourself, but in reality, your win rate is going to be very low. The ads we're going to focus on today are going to have very high win rates. So instead of duplicating your best performing ads, we're going to be way more focused on a combination of new concepts, iterations, and variations, which are all very different things in the newest Andromeda updates and gem algorithmic changes to meta. So let's talk through the new way of doing this. So to start our system, what we're going to be building is a creative flywheel. This is going to be a predictable system that pumps out winning ads. So of course, at the top of every single creative machine or creative flywheel are new ads. And to source those new ads, they're going to come from two different places. And we're going to start from the single most important place. And that of course is going to be your competitors. Now, there's a free way to do this and there's a paid way to do this. I'm going to use the paid way. You could use the free way. I'm going to show you both really simply. First, the free way. We go into Facebook ads library. We click all ads and you go ahead and search one by one each of the competitors that are most relevant to your business. So, in this example, I'm just going to pretend that I'm the brand Vori. They're a sportsware kind of athleisure brand. One of their main competitors is Lululemon. So, what I would do if I was Viori is I would type in Lululemon. We're then going to select their page and we're able to see every single ad that Lululemon is currently running. And as you can see right here, they have hundreds of active ads in their account right now. So, I'm trying to think and clock what of these can I use as inspiration. What you really want to do is look at what ads have either been live the longest or spent the most. So, obvious things you could look out for are anything that says low impression count. You could very well and easily know that that is not a high performing ad. Or you could scroll all the way down to the bottom, which might take a minute depending on what brand you're looking at and look for ads that have been spending for the longest period of time. Now, what I like to do is use a program called Magic Brief. This is a paid platform. We're not sponsored by them, but it's the easiest way to show you everything. And we can see Lululemon right here is running 2382 active ads. We can see a quick overview of all the ads that they're running. And I could scroll through everything really easy. And I could download all of this imagery if I want to. Now, you might notice this looked a little bit different than Facebook ads library. And that's because they're running ads from different pages. So on the ad library, you might have to search through a variety of different pages from Lululemon and you might have to change the active status to all available ads because some of their ads might be paused after certain periods of time. And I want to give you a pro tip here. If you're a small brand and you're in the athletic leisure space, do not compare yourself to Lululemon. Don't compare yourself to Nike. Think about brands that are a step or two above you. If you're doing a million dollars in revenue, think of a brand that's doing 10 million. find and strike that balance between brands that are not too big. I'm never going to take inspiration from Nike, but not too small where they're not driving any sales, of course. So, once we find the brand and the creative that we are interested in, what we're looking for are the ads that have run the longest. We're looking for ads that have been most active for this brand. And I'm looking for real concepts here. Now, let's use this ad concept by Lululemon, which has run for 469 days. is they launched this in October of 2024. I am able to now take this ad, this carousel that they've developed here and use this as inspiration. We can recreate this very easily if I was Viori. So now in this example here, I'm just adding inspiration from competitive ads. You should be taking their videos, their statics, their gifts, their carousels, and build a true collection of concepts that you can identify. Each of these three are completely different concepts. You should be able to note and expand that each of these can be heavily expanded on. You should extrapolate out dozens of different iterations of this. You can make this exact ad if I was VRE versus Lululemon for every single product if I know it's a winning concept. But keep in mind, this is just scratching the surface. You can do this for every single one of your competitors. Identify trends and find common threads of creative that generally work in your category. Then take those threads, take those concepts and build them for yourself. Once you've created the concepts from your competitors, you've built them for yourselves. You've then launched your own new ads. What do you do next? This part is going to sound a little too easy. You wait. But it's not just about waiting. You have to make sure things are set up properly with those new ads to be able to have that luxury to actually wait and be patient. Now, we like to launch all of our new ads inside of a prospecting CBO campaign. The idea here is pretty simple. We want competition within our own ad account. And that works in a very simple way. Every time we have new creatives, they get launched into a new ad set. It could be anywhere from two creatives, one creative, 10 creatives, 15 creatives. Generally, four to eight creatives is the sweet spot. But don't over complicate it. Every time new ads get launched, they get launched into a new ad set.
